newsitem.title: GERMANY: German cooperative banks see no inflation dangers.
newsitem.headline: German cooperative banks see no inflation dangers.

text.p: Germany's cooperative banks said on Thursday there were no "home-made" factors or pressure from international markets that could be seen fuelling inflation for some time.

"The perspective for lasting price stability in Germany ... is currently more favourable than it has been for decades," the Federation of German Industrial and Agricultural Credit Cooperatives said in an economic review.

The report said there were no recognisable pressures from consumer prices and that M3 money supply growth, although expected to overshoot the Bundesbank target corridor this year, was "largely contributing to price stability."
Over the medium-term M3 growth was moderate and wages were also not growing too fast.
"Because German industry has sufficient capacity at its disposal, even strengthened economic recovery would hardly push up prices," the federation said.

The report said that these factors justified current low capital market interest rates and that continued federal budget discipline and a tight Bundesbank monetary policy could create more room for lower rates.
The only significant danger was the prospect that the United States could raise interest rates.
"The German market would hardly be able to fully sidestep this influence," the report said.

The report also pointed out that interest rate differntials between southern European countries recently had fallen drastically and it saw this as a foreshadow of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"Apparently there is speculation these countries will be early participants in monetary union," the report said. "But with a strict reading of the convergence criteria they would hardly have a realistic chance of participating at the start."
